prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: All six of us ranked GLP-1 first, and the case rests on more than agreement. It is a complete chain from basic physiology (incretin secretion and action, proglucagon processing, the identity of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide) to a drug class with large randomized outcome evidence in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. It has decades of independent confirmation, so the recognition is mature. A citation centred on the physiology and the active peptide fits the prize's physiological emphasis. It also leaves room to note that development of long-acting analogues followed from that biology.
statement.case_against: Credit is the weak point. Habener and others are outside the supplied names, and the contribution of Mojsov versus the industrial development teams is disputed. Dropping Knudsen, as I now propose, leaves out the person who designed liraglutide and semaglutide, which are the drugs patients actually use. A prize for physiology that skips drug design can look incomplete when the public impact comes from the analogues. My own opening ballot made the opposite trade-off, so I regard this as a close call and not a settled one.

responses.point: Perlmann holds that Drucker, Holst and Mojsov are the most defensible scientific trio. He treats Knudsen's contribution as largely pharmaceutical development and notes the Eshhar gap under CAR-T.
responses.response: I moved toward this view. In my opening ballot I preferred Knudsen over Mojsov because the analogue design is what turned the physiology into therapy. His point is that the prize should reward what was discovered about the hormone, and identifying the active peptide form is a discovery in that sense. Acylated analogue design is an engineering achievement built on it. I still think leaving out Knudsen is a real cost, but I accept it for a three-person limit. I agree with his CAR-T concern, since Eshhar's absence is a real attribution problem for B006.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, on the grounds that Knudsen led the design of the long-acting analogues. She also ranks TNF blockade (B018) and HPV vaccines (B016) highly.
responses.response: I take her argument seriously, because it was my own opening position. I now disagree with it on one point. If Knudsen's analogue work is counted as the decisive step, then the Holst and Drucker part of the citation also becomes a story about therapy. That blurs the line between this prize and pharmaceutical awards. I also think Mojsov's role in identifying the active peptide is more defensible than her answer implies, even with the dispute. On B018 I partly disagree with her ranking. Feldmann and Maini have strong clinical proof and long maturity, but I rank it below CAR-T and optogenetics on conceptual originality, since anti-cytokine therapy became broadly established through many contributors.

responses.point: The chair ranked imatinib (B024) second and HPV vaccines (B016) third, citing clear originality, decades of survival data and population-level cancer prevention. He also notes the Lasker recognition and priority complications for HPV.
responses.response: I agree that imatinib is among the cleanest examples of rational targeted therapy, and its maturity is not in doubt. My reservation is that the prize question is whether it adds a new concept beyond what earlier prizes already covered, and the BCR-ABL translocation and oncogene work behind it is credited elsewhere. I also read the HPV priority dispute involving Zhou as a more serious fairness risk than he implies. I would not push either ahead of GLP-1, but I would keep B024 as a credible later candidate.

responses.point: Sandberg proposes a two-person CAR-T prize for June and Sadelain, leaving out Rosenberg because adoptive cell transfer is a distinct contribution.
responses.response: I partly disagree. Dropping Rosenberg gives a cleaner story about CAR design, but it leaves out the adoptive cell transfer work that made engineered T cells credible as a therapy, and I included him in my opening ballot. Given the Eshhar problem, I think any CAR-T configuration is fragile whichever names are chosen. For that reason I would not support a CAR-T prize in the same year as GLP-1, and I regard it as the main alternative for a later year.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen is the better third name alongside Drucker and Holst, and how far the unresolved Habener credit dispute should affect the choice.
Whether a physiology-centred citation can acknowledge the analogue drugs without making Knudsen necessary.
Whether CAR-T can be given a defensible attribution without Eshhar, who is not among the supplied names.
Whether optogenetics (B049) can be reduced to three credited names without an unfair omission among Bamberg, Boyden, Hegemann, Nagel, Deisseroth and Miesenböck.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. My documented co-authorship (spatial transcriptomics, single-cell work) does not involve any credited name on the shortlist, and shared Karolinska affiliation alone is not treated as a tie.
